title: Częstochowa
hookLine: Poland's Black Madonna, an icon with scars on her cheek

lines: TWO CUTS ON A PAINTED CHEEK.
cards: Two thin cuts run down a woman's right cheek, and a third crosses them, like a scar that healed badly.
They're on a painting: a dark icon of Mary holding her child, kept in a monastery on a hill in the Polish city of Częstochowa.
Her face is solemn and dark brown, almost black, which is why people call her the Black Madonna. Her son sits on her arm, one hand raised. A precious image, and nobody has made it look new.
Why would anyone keep the wound?

teach.b: Start with the stories. Tradition says Saint Luke painted it, on a tabletop from the house in Nazareth.

Art historians argue about when and where it was really made, and Catholics are free to hold the legend lightly; it's a story people tell, not something the Church asks anyone to believe. Then the scars.
Tradition says raiders once broke into the monastery and tried to carry the icon off, and when it wouldn't go, one of them struck her face with a sword.
The image was repaired, but the cuts were left, or came back, depending on who tells it. And the dark color? Smoke from candles, age, the paint itself; people still debate it.
Next, the country. Tradition says that when the monastery held out against an invading army, Poland's king named Mary queen of Poland.
Through wars and hard years after, Poles kept coming to this hill, and pilgrims still walk there on foot, singing as they go. Last, the scars again.
In the Book of Lamentations, a ruined city speaks to everyone who walks past her.
In the Douay-Rheims: "O all ye that pass by the way, attend, and see if there be any sorrow like to my sorrow."

teach.h: SEE IF THERE BE ANY SORROW LIKE TO MY SORROW.
teach.b: Some readers have heard Mary in that voice. A pilgrim before this icon does what the verse asks: stops, and looks at the wound. The cut isn't damage to be hidden.
For pilgrims from a country that knew invasion, she could be a mother who had been hurt too, and stayed.

how: Catholics venerate the icon of Our Lady of Częstochowa at the Jasna Góra monastery in Poland, where pilgrims come to pray before it, some walking there on foot, and copies of the icon hang in Polish churches and homes elsewhere.

games.q: you're repairing a precious icon of Mary. raiders have slashed her face. what do you do with the cuts?
o: paint them over so she looks new.
leave the scars on her cheek.
replace the whole painting with a copy.
games.why: the scars stayed. for pilgrims who had known invasion and loss, a mother with a wound on her face asked what Lamentations asks: attend, and see.

practice: Bring to mind Poland, or one person from it, and the pilgrims on the road to that hill, tired and singing, walking toward a scarred face. Then let your mind move to anyone you know who carries a wound that hasn't been painted over.
If you pray, say a Hail Mary for Poland and for them; if not, simply hold them in mind, kindly.

wordCard.voice: Częstochowa. The Polish city whose monastery keeps the Black Madonna, an icon of Mary with scars across her cheek, honored as a mother by the pilgrims who walk to it. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the scarred icon. The wound was kept, not painted over. See you tomorrow.
